steps.text: **Why the pawn move hurts.** A pawn cannot retreat, so the skeleton it leaves lasts for the whole game (Edward Lasker's point, paraphrased [V-sheet]). Closing a wing is right when your pieces already have good squares or when the other side's break is the real danger. [I] Here neither held: Black's pieces had no outpost, White's had one. Before you lock a wing, ask which squares you stop guarding.

steps.chapter: Mistake 2: the quiet move in a race

steps.prompt: In a race, when would a quiet move be right? Give one example in your own words.

fields.label: A quiet move is right when:

steps.text: **Tempo in a race.** A tempo is one move. If both sides race and a quiet move starts neither plan, the opponent gains a move for free. Znosko-Borovsky advises, against a time lead, to keep making small threats (paraphrased [V-sheet]); a waiting move does the opposite. [H] A quiet move is right only when the opponent's plan is slower than yours by more than that one move. [I] Whether it is, you count: the next board counts it.

steps.caption: ONE LINE, not the engine's choice at every move: only the end is engine-read (depth 16). Two quiet black moves (12...a6, 13...b6) against 13.Nd3 and 14.b4 end between +1.5 and +2.0 pawns, from +0.5 to +1.1 at the start: about a pawn for two quiet moves. A single quiet move costs only a few tenths, inside the noise of depth 16.

steps.text: **Why the king step is slow.** The pawn storm needs pieces behind it; the king step answers no threat and starts no plan [I]. On f1 the king stays on the f-file, where the pawn landing on g3 attacks the bishop on f2 and the pawn on h2 with tempo. The engine prefers a piece that does something, by about half a pawn. After your move ask: what does the opponent want next, and have I changed it? (Znosko-Borovsky, paraphrased [V-sheet]: how to defend depends on what you have lost.)

steps.text: **Two tests of the repair rule.** Znosko-Borovsky, paraphrased [V-sheet]: when you stand worse, defend and restore freedom; but he also warns that playing actively from a worse position is the most dangerous choice. In these two positions the engine's first choice kept the attack alive [V, depth 16]. [I] Two positions do not overturn his advice. They show that counterplay can work while many pieces are near the enemy king. [H] Where the attack has no pieces left, defend.

steps.text: **Check the answer before you capture.** The overlooked candidate does most of the damage in calculation, according to a reviewer's account of Aagaard's book [S, paraphrased]. [I] Here the capture looked natural because the rook attacked a piece, and the pawn push attacked a rook and threatened to queen. Ask three questions before any capture: who defends the piece, what does the recapture open, and which quiet move did I not list?

**The repair table.** Each mistake and the repair that scored best in its position; each rests on one position [I].
- Closed the queenside with ...c5: that gave White d5. Check which squares you stop guarding.
- Quiet move in a race: here two cost about a pawn.
- Stepped aside under a storm: here a knight strike scored better.
- Gave material: counterplay scored better in two positions, though the source calls it risky.
- Captured first: count the defenders, list candidates.
